5.98.m:
Sūta said:
Having heard this speech of Dharmarāja, the brahmin
again asked concerning the auspicious rule for the month of Mādhava.

The brahmin said:
O Dharmarāja of great fortune, the secret has been properly revealed:
the supreme merit arising from the Mādhava bath, which bestows liberation on mortals.

Having bathed at dawn, composed in mind, in the month of Mādhava,
how should one worship the god Mādhava, and with which flowers? State that rule!

Dharmarāja said:
Among all kinds of leaves, tulasī is dear to Keśava.
Sacred places like Puṣkara, and rivers like the Gaṅgā,

and the gods headed by Vāsudeva abide in the tulasī leaf.
Always and at all times, tulasī is beloved of Viṣṇu.

Leaving aside the mālatī flower, and leaving the lotus,
one should take a tulasī leaf and worship Mādhava with devotion.

Even Śeṣa would not be able to declare the fruit of his merit.
If one gathers tulasī without having bathed, for a rite to the gods or an ancestral ceremony,

all of that becomes fruitless, and one is purified only by pañcagavya.
Poverty, the experience of sorrow, and very many sins—

tulasī removes them quickly, just as the harītakī removes diseases.
Tulasī is known as dark and light; having worshipped the enemy of Madhu with it,

a man, as a devotee of Hari in particular, becomes Nārāyaṇa.
Because he who worships the slayer of Madhu with tulasī throughout the entire month of Mādhava

at the three junctures of the day, has no rebirth.
In the absence of flowers and leaves, one may even worship with food and the like,

always [worshipping] Hari with grains of rice, wheat, or barley,
having bathed at dawn according to rule in Mādhava, the month dear to Mādhava.

One should offer libations to the ancestors, gods, men, and the moving and unmoving creation.
He who constantly sprinkles the base of an aśvattha tree with abundant water,

should then circumambulate it, which consists of all the gods.
He who worships the divine aśvattha tree on all sides with water—
by him ten thousand families are saved; of this there is no doubt.

Misfortune, ill omen, bad dreams, and ill thoughts—
all sorrow dissolves through the libation to the aśvattha, dear friend.

By him the ancestors are gratified, by him Viṣṇu is worshipped;
by that hero who worships the aśvattha, the planetary deities are worshipped as well.

One should touch white horses, flowers, the śamī tree, fire, sandalwood, the solar orb,
and the aśvattha tree, and then perform the duties of one's own caste.

Scratching a cow, offering food to a cow, bathing, offering libations to the pippala tree,
and performing worship of Govinda: doing this, one never reaches a bad state.

On the thirteenth, fourteenth, and full moon day of Vaiśākha, for three days,
even one entirely incapacitated, whether woman or man,

observing the previously mentioned rules, bathing at dawn according to one's capacity,
is freed from all mortal sins and enjoys imperishable heaven.

On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one should feed ten brahmins according to one's capacity.
Having risen after a fast of three nights, bathing just once, restrained and pure,

having given light-colored or black sesame seeds mixed with honey
to twelve brahmins, one should have them pronounce blessings on that very day:

'May Dharmarāja be pleased with me!' and one should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods.
The sin committed throughout one's entire life is destroyed at that very instant.

He shall dwell comfortably in the heavenly realm for many myriads of years.
Worshipped by all deities, he will never see me [as judge of the dead].

Cooked food, water pitchers, and the like, for the gratification of the ancestors and the gods,
on the thirteenth, fourteenth, and the full moon day, for three days—

whoever gives these with devotion, O brahmin, is freed from great sins.
Moreover, [offering] vessels of gold and sesame to brahmins according to capacity every day,
If he satiates [them] with vessels of water, he dispels the murder of a Brahmin. / On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, they were created by the Lotus-born [Brahmā];
and sesamum seeds should be given with devotion for the sake of fortune and lineage. / Hear now, O observer of vows, the ancient event in this matter,
the exceedingly wondrous fruit of the full moon of the month of Mādhava. / Beginning with the entrance [of the sun] into Aries, the thirty lunar days are supreme;
they are proclaimed in the Purāṇas as meritorious and greater than all sacrifices. / Especially those three are pure and difficult for a sinner to attain.
Even more meritorious than those is the full moon of Mādhava, dear to Mādhava; / this initial lunar day, the beginning of the Vārāha Kalpa, yields great fruit.
Formerly on this [day], Nārāyaṇa deluded the two primal Daityas, / Hiraṇyākṣa and Madhu, O Brahmin, and the earth was raised up.
On the thirteenth, fourteenth, and the full moon day, this all-pervading Lord / performed these three in succession, in this bright fortnight of the month of Mādhava.
From then on, O chief of Brahmins, the full moon day especially / is declared purifying, the beginning of a kalpa, witnessing rites for a kalpa.
If one has not bathed in the morning with discipline in Vaiśākha, / what is the use of his birth, O Brahmin? Surely he harms his own self.
Particularly on the thirteenth, fourteenth, and the full moon day, / even a woman or a man, following the proper method,
who bathes in the morning with self-restraint, is freed from all sins. / One whose full moon day of Vaiśākha passes devoid of bath, gift, worship,
śrāddha rites, merit, and the like, certainly has his abode in hell. / There is no scripture equal to the Veda; there is no sacred bath equal to the Gaṅgā;
there is no gift equal to water and a cow; there is no lunar day equal to the full moon of Vaiśākha. / And whoever, intent on Viṣṇu, gives a water-cow on the full moon of Vaiśākha,
becomes a fourth in distinction even among the three gods. / Even a slayer of a mother, a slayer of a father, a slayer of an embryo, or a violator of the guru's bed,
is freed from all sins upon merely beholding the water-cow. / They deliver ten ancestors and ten descendants from hell.
Those who offer a water-cow according to the rite during these three [days] of Vaiśākha, / sugar, fruit, betel, shoes, hand-fans,
and give them to the foremost of the twice-born, are proclaimed fortunate here; / and jars of water, cooked food, and a sacrificial fee of gold,
whoever gives on the full moon of Vaiśākha obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice. / In this connection also they cite this ancient legendary history,
the dialogue of a Brahmin with spirits in a great forest. / Formerly in the Middle Country, O sinless one, there was a Brahmin named Dhanaśarman.
Having gone to the forest for kuśa grass and the like, he then saw this wonder: / terrified, he beheld three wicked and exceedingly dreadful spirits,
with hair standing erect, red eyes, black teeth, and emaciated bellies, / making various cries and running about hither and thither.
Seeing them, the Brahmin, trembling with fear, ran away swiftly; / wailing, they then pursued him.
Overwhelmed by those spirits, he spoke sweet words. / Dhanaśarman said: "Who are you? Whence has this state of yours, fit for hell, arisen?
You ought to protect me, afflicted with fear, pitiable, and distressed— / a Vaiṣṇava, a destitute Brahmin with many servants, who has come to the forest.
Keśava will surely grant fortune even to you; / the venerable Viṣṇu, benefactor of Brahmins, has been pleased with me out of compassion.
Viṣṇu, resembling the flax flower, is Hari clad in yellow garments, / by the mere hearing of whose name great darkness departs.
He is the beginningless and endless God, bearer of the conch, discus, and mace, / imperishable, lotus-eyed, the granter of liberation to departed spirits."
Yama said: / By the mere hearing of the name of Viṣṇu, those goblins were pleased; / resting in a virtuous state, restrained by compassion and courtesy,
gladdened by his speech and urged by his instruction, / the spirits, tormented by the flood of hunger and thirst, spoke this to the twice-born.
The spirits said: / "By your very sight, O Brahmin, and from hearing the name of Hari, / we have attained another state of mind and have become compassionate.
Association with a Vaiṣṇava indeed removes misfortune, / joins one with fortune, and swiftly spreads fame.
Made of elixir, cooling, bestowing supreme bliss, / whom indeed does the moonlight of Vaiṣṇava nectar not delight?
This one is named 'Ungrateful'; this second one is 'Without God'; / and this third is 'Without Vaiśākha', the sinner among all three.
Always did he practice extreme ungratefulness through sin; / therefore, his name derived from his deeds has been fixed as 'Kṛtaghna' [Ungrateful].
In a previous birth he was a Śūdra named Sudāsa. / By that sin of ungratefulness, O twice-born, he reached this state.
For an extreme sinner, a rogue, and one harmful to guru or master, / an expiation exists, O brāhmaṇa, but for the ungrateful there is no expiation.
Having experienced a multitude of various hells with bodies capable of torment, / he has now reached this final state, O twice-born.
He always ate food without performing worship of the gods / and without giving to gurus and brāhmaṇas; therefore he is 'Vidaivata' [Godless].
He was a king, the lord of ten thousand villages, / known by the name Harivīra in a previous birth.
Driven by anger, arrogance, and atheism, intent on transgressing the guru's command, / he ate without performing the great sacrifices, reviling brāhmaṇas.
By that sinful deed, having experienced the agony of great hells, / he became a ghost named Vidaivata.
I, Avaiśākha [Non-Vaiśākha-observer], am the third, a sinner among the three; / therefore my name was established by my deed, though I was a brāhmaṇa.
Born in Madhyadeśa, Gautamī by clan, / I was a sacrificer brāhmaṇa residing in Vāsapura in a previous birth.
Solely following the Vedic path alone, / I never bathed in the month of Mādhava with the god Mādhava in mind.
Nothing was given or offered in fire by me, especially on the full-moon day of Vaiśākha; / the slayer of Madhu was not worshipped then, nor were wise men gratified.
Neither were the ancestral spirits and gods gratified with water pots, water jars, and gifts, / nor were sesame seeds mixed with honey given to learned brāhmaṇas.
Learned men were not honored then with flowers, fruits, betel, sandalwood, fans, and garments / for the pleasure of ancestors and deities.
Not even one full-moon day of Vaiśākha, granting full fruits, was observed by me / through the meritorious deeds of bathing, charity, rites, and worship.
Therefore, all my Vedic ritual action was indeed completely fruitless; / hence I have become a ghost named Avaiśākha in all respects.
All this cause concerning all three of us has been told to you; / do you become our deliverer from sin, since you are indeed a brāhmaṇa.
Because the holy water of Brahman is released, and good men are supreme, / they deliver from great sin, and even from hells, those who take refuge in them.
Between a man who always bathes in sacred waters such as the Gaṅgā / and one who keeps company with the virtuous, association with the virtuous is superior.
Or rather, I have a son renowned as Dhanaśarman; / going to him, awaken him, O master, to make an effort for our sake.
Making an effort when the need of others presents itself, / one obtains abundant fruit, greater than sacrificial rites and gift-giving.
Yama said: / Having heard the ghost's words, Dhanaśarman was deeply grieved, / realizing that his own father had fallen into hell.
Censuring himself completely, he spoke this word: / Dhanaśarman said: / "O master, I am your son, yet useless to Gautama.
A son who does not unweariedly effect the deliverance of his father / cannot purify himself; he is called a non-giver though possessing wealth.
Dharma is indeed deep and difficult to know even with effort by a wise man, / since you, my father, have reached such an evil state.
And since you have obtained no succession of happiness from me / in either of the two worlds, how can I be considered a good son?
Two are the gurus of a person here according to dharma: father and mother; / even between them, the father is superior, in view of the primacy of the seed.
What shall I do? Where shall I go? How can you find a good state, father? / I do not know the truth of dharma; I rely on your word."
The ghost said: / "Listen, O son, to my true word, through the force of what is to come: / now, by some merit, my good state shall come to be.
While performing Vedic rites, indeed out of pride / the word of the guru was disregarded by me, and the guru was insulted there.
By disrespecting gurus, through arrogance, anger, and conceit, / meritorious deeds go to ruin, just as reputations do through bad conduct.
Whatever rite is according to Purāṇic prescription, not in conflict with Vedic scripture, [was ignored], / and only Vedic rites alone were performed by me out of ignorance.
Not a single full-moon day of Vaiśākha—a forest fire to the firewood of sin, / an axe to the tree of sin—was performed by me according to rule, O son.
A man whose Vaiśākha passes without vows becomes an 'Avaiśākha'; / he is then born for ten lifetimes in animal wombs.
After suffering grief for a long time, in the end he becomes a ghost in turn, / and only with difficulty does he somehow attain human birth.
I shall tell you a supreme remedy that effects release from the state of a ghost, / which I heard in a previous birth from the mouth of my own guru.

Go home, my son, and having bathed in the Yamunā according to rule— / for today, granting every goal, that commencement of the kalpa has also arrived; / on the western day, the full moon of Vaiśākha is beneficial for worshipping ancestors and gods.
Even water mixed with sesame seeds, together with water pots, food, and fruits, with devotion / one should give to the ancestors; by that, a śrāddha given for a thousand years is effected here.
Whoever feeds the gods of the earth on the full-moon day of Vaiśākha, / at every mouthful there will be satisfaction for the ancestors for the number of a yuga.
Having bathed according to rule on the full-moon day of Vaiśākha, if one feeds ten brāhmaṇas / with milk-rice pudding, he is freed from all sins; there is no doubt about this.
Giving either white or black sesame seeds mixed with honey / to ten brāhmaṇas, he should have them pronounce blessings.
Saying 'May Dharmarāja be pleased,' he should gratify the ancestors and gods; / the sin committed throughout a lifetime is destroyed that very moment.
Sesame seeds were created by the Lotus-born on the full-moon day of Vaiśākha; / they should be given with devotion, and touched over the entire body, O twice-born.
Whoever bathes with sesame seeds mixed with barley over the whole body then, / to him Brahmā and Dharma grant their desired boon here.
Whoever gives water pots for the pleasure of Dharmarāja, / by him seven and seven generations are delivered; of this there is no doubt.
On the thirteenth, fourteenth, and the full-moon day, intent on devotion, / having bathed, chanted mantras, offered oblation, given gifts, and worshipped Mādhava—
whatever fruit arises, O son, bestow that upon us! / I will not take refuge in going to heaven abandoning these two familiar ghosts.
Indeed, the end of the sin of these two as well has arrived." / Yama said: / Having said "So be it," that brāhmaṇa departed and then did all of that.
Pleased, with supreme devotion he performed bathing and gift-giving on the full moon of Vaiśākha; / having bathed, gladdened with devotion, having attained the Mādhava full moon,
giving many gifts, he bestowed the merit separately upon them. / That very instant, they all mounted celestial chariots and went to heaven.
Rejoicing by the application of that transfer of merit, O best of twice-born, / Dhanaśarman, too, a lord of brāhmaṇas, knower of Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇa,
having enjoyed pleasures for a long time, attained the world of Brahmā. / Therefore this full moon of Vaiśākha, the most holy, is the purifier of the universe.
It is told by me in brief, O brāhmaṇa, on account of its great weight.

Blessed are they, and successful are they born in the world; they alone are the men who attain the goals of life, / who, plunging into water in the morning with purified minds and restrained observance, worship the slayer of Madhu in the month of Mādhava.
The mortal who, having bathed at dawn in the month of Mādhava, worships the Lord of Ramā, / endowed with moral restraints and engaged in all religious vows, surely destroys sin.
By them alone has Time been conquered; they alone are blessed among men, free from sins; / they alone do not enter the womb again who, devoted, bathe in the month of Mādhava.
That Mādhava resounds through conjunction with sacrifice, through the performance of austerity and gifts; / in which month, howsoever small the merit performed here, it becomes equal to a kalpa.
For of the man plunging [into water] at sunrise in Mādhava to worship Mādhava, / even a dark body, from contact with drops of water, brings about purification.
Ascending the body of an embodied being, those sins wander about only so long / as this cosmic form, named Mādhava and beloved of the lover of Ramā, does not arrive.
Fierce and numerous sins equal to Mounts Meru and Mandara, / the month of Mādhava, dear to Mādhava, burns when one has bathed.
This has been spoken by me in brief out of grace to you, O twice-born, / the glorification of bathing in Vaiśākha, which destroys the sin of the hearer.
Whoever will hear with devotion this legendary history uttered by me, / he too, delivered from sin, will not see me [in judgment].
Even sins like killing a Brahmin, although committed many times, / are certainly destroyed by the ritual of Vaiśākha.
One who has bathed according to rule in Vaiśākha delivers ancestors from hell: / thirty prior, thirty subsequent, and thirty after that.
On one side are all sacred places and all sacrifices with their fees; / on the other is the month of Mādhava observed with vows.
Because to that Lord Hari of exalted deeds / this month of Mādhava is dear, superior and greater than all.
Do not harbour any doubt in any way, O earthly god [Brahmin], / concerning the month of Vaiśākha, which has been spoken by me in summary.
In this matter, hear that wondrous ancient event; / although not to be told, I shall narrate this short tale to you."

5.99.m: Yama said: / Formerly there was a king known by the name of Mahīratha, / who obtained abundant treasures of sovereignty as the fruit of prior merit.
He stayed solely caressed by women, occupied with erotic art, / addicted solely to that vice, not established in dharma and wealth.
Having placed the royal fortune in his minister, the king enjoyed the objects of sense; / accompanied by beautiful women, he was averse to the affairs of the kingdom.
He saw neither subjects nor wealth, neither dharma nor purpose nor duty, / having impressions solely suited to sports and dalliance with lovely women.
Then after a long time, his family priest, Kaśyapa, / spoke righteous words to him, thinking thus in his mind:
"The guru who out of delusion does not restrain a king from adharma, / he too shares in that sin; therefore, he must be instructed by the family priest."
If, even when warned, he disregards the word of the royal priest, / the royal priest is blameless in that matter, and the king incurs all the guilt.
Listen, O King, to the word of my teacher, which is endowed with righteousness and purpose, / consistent in meaning, full of purpose, and free from desire, passion, and the like.
Standing by the word of the teacher is indeed the supreme dharma; / even a fraction of the teacher’s command increases the lifespan, glory, and happiness of kings.
You have not satisfied the Brāhmaṇas with gifts, nor have you worshipped Viṣṇu; / you have performed no vow, no penance whatever, and certainly no pilgrimage.
Under the sway of desire, you have not contemplated the name of Hari. / Alas, consorting with timid women, you have not sought the company of the learned.
To whom are beloved women, bearing the chowries of the god of love, not dear? / Yet they are as unstable as the leaf of a banana plant agitated by the wind.
High-minded men are not satisfied with riches as flickering as waves, / with pleasures as fleeting as the knit of a brow, or with youth to be enjoyed for but an instant.
What is the use of learning and penance, what of renunciation or prudent policy, / what of a solitary mind to one whose mind has been stolen by women?
Dharma is the only friend who follows one in death; / everything else goes to destruction along with the body.
One should accumulate dharma gradually, as ants build an anthill; / for with dharma as one’s companion, one crosses the darkness that is hard to cross.
As fickle as the surge of towering waves driven by the wind, / do you not know, O sovereign of kings, the deceptive illusion of men's lives?
For those whose jeweled crown is humility, whose earrings are truth and dharma, / and whose bracelet is generosity—what need have they for inert ornaments?
Leaving the dead body on the ground like a log or a clod of earth, / kinsmen turn their faces away and depart; dharma follows him.
When all things are passing away, when life is thus waning, / and when existence is slipping away, why do you not rise and run?
Family, sons, wives, and the rest, the body, and the accumulation of wealth / belong to others and are transient; only good deeds and bad deeds are truly one's own.
Since you must depart helplessly, leaving everything behind, / why are you attached to what is worthless and do not practice your own dharma?
Without resting place, without support, without provisions for the journey, without a guide, / how will you, once dead, walk the wilderness path alone?
For when you have departed, no one will follow behind you; / only your good deeds and your bad deeds will follow you as you go.
Perform without sloth the beneficial action declared by Śruti and Smṛti, / suitable for your family and country, the root of dharma, and righteous conduct.
One should abandon material wealth and sensual pleasure if they are devoid of dharma; / through dharma everything is attained: wealth, pleasure, and happiness.
One should practice the conquest of the senses and yoga day and night; / for one who has conquered his senses is able to establish his subjects on the right path.
Fortunes, as fickle as the side-glances of wanton women, / remain long with kings through humility and disciplined application.
Of the foolish whose nature is desire, pride, and the like, who act without reflection, / their fortunes perish together with their lifespan.
High-minded men do not dance with joy over fortunes seen and lost; / the ocean is neither filled by incoming rivers nor drained by outgoing ones.
Between vice and death, vice is said to be the more painful; / the vicious king sinks lower and lower, while the king free from vice goes to heaven.
Vices lead to ruin, especially those born of lust; / therefore, O great king, abandon lust, which is opposed to dharma.
Kingdoms enjoyed by destiny belong even to the dull-witted, the indiscriminate, / demons, evil-minded men, and also the unrighteous.
They are never stable here when attended by sins; / they dissolve just as fuel does in contact with fire.
Whether walking, standing, awake, or sleeping, / he whose mind is not devoted to discernment is truly dead.
Because he is an instructor of those learned in sacred lore, he is called a teacher; / yet teachings are like hair on the head to those whose misfortunes are imminent.
Leaving aside the fever of sensual objects with an even and healthy mind, / and with practical discernment, a wise man accomplishes his own welfare.
Wandering from the impure, it goes to the pure, and from that to the other again; / the mind of a living creature is like a child, so one should turn it away by force.
Reflecting upon the thought of the elders who see dharma, O King, / one should restrain with supreme intellect the mind that wanders onto evil paths.
Neither riches help, nor friends, nor relatives, / nor moving hand and foot, nor traveling to foreign lands.
Neither the misery of bodily affliction nor resorting to sacred shrines [helps]; / the supreme state is attained solely through the recitation of one whose mind is fixed on that.
Therefore, when the mind wanders among sensual objects, a wise man should strive / to control it, O King, just as a firm driver controls horses.
You should do whatever is necessary, O King, so that you are not deceived / by the sages and by those various fruits; listen now to that.
Even when bewildered, a man should consult wise friends; / and as they advise when consulted, that should be done properly.
By every means, the restraint of desire and anger must be undertaken / by one who desires the highest good; for both are bent on destroying one's welfare.
For desire is powerful, O King, a great enemy residing in the body; / a person who desires the highest good must not fall under its sway.
That desire which was formerly burned by the trident-bearing god of gods / with the fire of his forehead, and made bodiless—such is the established truth.
When that mind-born god desires to destroy a woman, / he enters the body of men and shows his true nature.
As a man continually contemplates the form of a woman, / [desire], resting upon that unseen form, drives the man mad.
In the same way, this [desire] drives the limb of a woman mad, without doubt; / therefore, O King, he came to be called Smara from remembrance.
Whatever color clothes a hero wears, / through the radiance of his own splendor, it would become fit to drink with streams of tears.
Mounting the form of a woman, it bewilders even a steadfast man; / and resorting to a man, it melts a woman.
He alone is innate, O King, bodiless yet dwelling in the body; / how is sin assigned even to the tiny body, O Lord?
Upon contacting which even the purest things, the five products of the cow and sacrificial offerings, / instantly become impure—what else could be more impure than that?
Even while smelling his own foul odor and seeing his own filth, / this person does not become detached, even while pinching his nose.
Upon contacting which delicious food and drinks, though fragrant, / quickly become impure—what else could be more impure than that?
Food that has entered the stomach abandons its own form; / mixed with worms, its impurity is quickly recognized indeed.
Even so in the body, O King, it abandons its own nature; / thereafter it truly attains the state of dog-filth, swarming with worms and foul stench.
There indeed lice and worms are born, without doubt; / that worm causes eruptions and an intense itching.
It produces severe pain and causes the whole body to twitch; / when scratched with the tips of fingernails, that itching is soothed.
In the same way, the pleasure of sexual intercourse arises, without doubt; / thus a mortal consumes savors, eats good food, and drinks again.
The internal fire cooks what is there and expels waste through the apāna; / and the essence, the fluid, becomes stimulated there.
Pure and spotless, the semen goes to the seat of Brahman; / drawn by the samāna breath, it is led by that very wind.
The semen finds no resting place, but remains in motion. / Indeed, within the skulls of living beings there are five worms,
two of them at the base of the ears, and then at the location of the eyes, / measured the size of a little finger, with red tails, O king,
having the colour of fresh butter, and with black tails, without doubt. / Listen from me as I tell their names, may it be well with you:
two worms named Piṅgalī and Śṛṅgalī are at the base of the ears; / Śṛṅgalī and Jaṅgalī, the other two, reside within the eyes.
There are one hundred and fifty similar worms, without doubt; / all of them reside within the forehead, the size of a mustard seed.
All suffering from skull-diseases become disordered, without doubt. / I shall speak of another thus: the great Prājāpatya worm,
the size of a grain of rice, and of that same colour, without doubt. / Two hairs exist at its mouth; listen, O king:
that intelligence of living beings decays from that very moment, without doubt; / even residing in its proper place, directly in the mouth of the Prājāpatya [worm],
that semen falls in the form of fluid, without doubt in this matter. / It drinks the semen with delight, and intoxicated by it, becomes wild.
Piercing the region of the palate, it continues in agitation. / The nāḍīs Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā reside there;
by its own force, the channel is shaken for a moment. / The itch of lust arises, O king, among all living beings indeed.
A man's phallus becomes erect, and a woman's vulva opens, O king; / both the woman and the man become intoxicated and then enter into union.
Rubbing body against body, it arises through sexual union; / there is pleasure for merely an instant, and then the same itch returns.
Everywhere this condition is seen, O hero, indeed of such a kind. / Tasteless is this culmination of sensual enjoyment, without doubt.
Dharma alone is the higher good when performed according to injunction. / Having taken recourse to steadfastness, therefore, practice dharma alone.
This breath is fickle, making hundreds of comings and goings in the midst of a moment; / the life of embodied beings is dependent on it: who would delay in dharma?
Though you have reached your tenth decade, O king, your mind even today / does not turn away from forbidden sense-objects—alas, alas!—fickle as it is.
Desire is never quenched by the enjoyment of desires; / like a fire with clarified butter, it only grows all the more.
Who else is capable of liberating a mind snatched away by an unchaste woman, / except the Lord who delights in the Self, the Blessed Mādhava?
Therefore, everything has come to futility through the impurity of lust; / yet your life remains now, O king: practice your own welfare.
I tell you, O king, what is the best of all the best for your welfare; / for I am your priest, sharing also in your good and bad deeds.
On the one side are all the merits for destroying the sins of sinners; / on the other side is the month of Mādhava, ever dear to Mādhava.
Killing a brāhmaṇa, drinking liquor, theft, and union with the teacher's wife— / these great sins alone have been proclaimed by the lords among sages.
Whatever [sin] has been committed by men with mind or body or even by a vow, / the month of Mādhava destroys all that, even the greatest darkness of sin.
Just as the sun destroys darkness on every side, O king, / so does the auspicious month of Mādhava; observe it according to rule.

Leaving behind those great, terrible sins committed since birth, O king, / mortals, through the merit born of observing the practices prescribed for the month of Vaiśākha, reach the abode of Hari in joy.
If they observe according to rule even one Vaiśākha / with faith, even sinners go to the abode of Hari in the end.
Therefore, you too, O best of kings, during this month of Mādhava now, / having bathed in the morning according to rule, worship the slayer of Madhu.
Just as the husk of a grain of rice, and just as the tarnish on copper, / are removed by ritual action, O hero, so is the impurity of a man.
Even the great innate impurity of the individual soul, like that of a grain of rice, / is indeed destroyed, there is no doubt; therefore perform the prescribed rite.

5.100.m: The glorious king said: / By your cool and spotless glances, like the water of the ocean of milk, / and by your true and wondrous words, I have been awakened.
Nectar not arisen from an ocean, an immaterial remedy for vice, / dispelling the affliction of mundane existence, has been given to me to drink by you, gentle one.
Bringing joy to men, causing the destruction of sin, a medicine for life, / removing old age and death, O brāhmaṇa, is association with the virtuous indeed.
Whatever desires are hard to attain on the surface of the earth, / all of them are obtained simply from the company of the virtuous.
For one who has bathed in the Ganges of association with the virtuous which takes away sin, / what need is there of gifts, what of holy bathing places, what of austerities, what of sacrifices?
For men sinking and rising in the ocean of mundane existence, the supreme refuge / is the virtuous who know dharma and are tranquil, like a sturdy boat for those drowning in the waters.
That disposition which was mine formerly, longing only for the pleasure of lust, / has today become reversed, O lord, from seeing you and from your word.
For the sake of the pleasure of one birth, one may ruin thousands [of births]; / a wise man, by means of one birth, gathers together thousands of births.
Alas, alas! With a mind longing for the pleasure of tasting the flavor of lust, / nothing for my own spiritual benefit was done by me, foolish as I was, O twice-born.
Ah, the delusion of my mind, by which the self, for the sake of women, / was cast into a terrible vice resulting in sorrow, difficult to overcome!
O venerable one, I am gratified, awakened by your word; / you should rescue me here by bestowing your instruction.
I must have performed merit in the past, since I have been awakened by you, / and have been purified especially even by the dust of your feet.
Tell me the rule for the month of Mādhava, O best among speakers, / which was proclaimed by you as bringing about the destruction of all sins.
What is the gift there, what is the bath, who is the deity, and what are the observances? / Declare this to me, O brāhmaṇa-seer, for my crossing over sins.
Yama said: / Thus addressed, the venerable Kaśyapa, a treasure-house of compassion, / spoke a righteous, universally beneficial, and auspicious word, O brāhmaṇa.
Kaśyapa said: / With an intellect capable of reconciling what precedes and what follows, O king, / you have asked; instruction should be given to a wise man, not to a base one with a sinful mind.
Likewise, having given auspicious understanding to one engaged in sin, O king, / the fruit of the gift of knowledge is properly attained, there is no doubt in this.
One should not speak to anyone unasked, nor to one who asks improperly; / even knowing, an intelligent person should act in the world like an ignorant fool.
Yet even unasked, the highest good and benefit should be spoken / to wise disciples, to sons, and to those engaged in rites who possess faith.
Now your heart has become pure through my word, / and through some merit performed in the past, O lord of the earth.
That body of yours which was in a state of sin has departed through taking refuge in me; / through hearing the dharmaśāstra, it has entered a state of righteousness.
The state of sin is called unrighteousness, devoid of the knowledge of dharma; / the other, which possesses good vows, should be known as righteous.
The third is beyond the senses, for experiencing dharma and adharma; / indeed, this threefold body is spoken of here by knowers of dharma.
to the extent that there is enjoyment of dharma and liberation; and this is threefold. / The body that is in a state of sin is called sinful.
Now, since you show devotion to the guru and listen to my words, / your body is established in the form of dharma.
By that alone, a spotless purity has arisen, suited for the rites of dharma. / Indeed, through destiny, the minds, deeds,
and bodies of embodied beings undergo change from time to time. / Presently, your mind certainly turns toward dharma;
therefore, I shall have you perform the supreme bath of Mādhava. / Yama said: Then, made to do so by that priest Kaśyapa,
that king [performed] bathing, giving, and worship in the month of Mādhava, / according to the injunction for bathing in Vaiśākha as seen in the ancient scriptures.
That sage spoke in return to the king, as prescribed, / and recited the essence of hymns, causing him to study that of Harimedhas,
upon hearing and studying which, one obtains the full fruit.
Having been guided by him, the king, pure in disposition, then duly performed / the praiseworthy rite in the glorious month of Mādhava, just as he had heard it with devotion:
the morning bath, water for washing the feet, water for offering, the worship of Hari, / and the food offering—the best of kings performed these with a devotional disposition.

Giving according to the rules, observing vows with devotion, he performs such an injunction in the month of Vaiśākha; / he who does so daily with devotion every year departs to Hari's abode, O best of earthly gods.
Then, in the other months, sporting with the breasts of lovely women, / he again became entirely eager for sensual enjoyment according to his desire.
He observed neither religious vows nor delved into royal affairs; / under the sway of passion, he neglected the month of Mādhava.
Even for the great, O best of Brahmins, passion is hard to restrain; / the sequence of latent impressions is indeed innate to the body and beginningless.
Shining with hair black as collyrium, difficult to touch, pleasing to the eyes, / women, like tongues of fire, burn a man as if he were grass.
Desire, residing in the body, is an awful enemy of men, as is well known; / made of the smoke of delusion and evil, whom does it not envelop in darkness?

5.101.m: Yama said: Then, regarded by the side-glance of Time, the king / died, his body emaciated by consumption arising from excessive sexual indulgence.
Led by the attendants of Yama, struck again and again, / weeping with great cries, he remembered his own sins.
The messengers of Viṣṇu, having arrived and struck my followers, / said, “This man is righteous,” and placed him upon a celestial chariot.
Praised by hosts of apsarases, the king was led to Hari's city, / his sins diminished by the morning bath of the month of Vaiśākha.
Then, thinking, “This man is devoid of dharma,” / by the command of Viṣṇu, those divine messengers / brought the king nearby the path of hell.
As he was going, he heard the varied cries / of weeping souls being boiled in hell.
Hearing the most dreadful wailing of sinners being cooked, / the king, filled with wonder, became exceedingly distressed, O Brahmin.
He said: “Messengers, what is this dreadful wailing that was heard / and is now heard no more? You ought to tell me the reason for this.”
The messengers said: Creatures who have abandoned proper conduct, sinful and devoid of good practice, / have been cast into the terrible hells, such as Tāmisra and others.
Those who have committed sins, after relinquishing their life-breaths, / take to the path of Yama and suffer terrible distress here.
Dragged here and there by the terrible servants of Yama, / fallen into darkness, they are eaten by extremely fearsome
dogs, jackals, carnivores, crows, herons, and cranes, / fire-beaked wolves, tigers, serpents, and scorpions.
They are burned with fire, pierced with thorns, / cut with saws, and afflicted with thirst.
Afflicted by hunger and hosts of terrible diseases, / they faint at every step from the stench of pus and blood.
In some places they are boiled in oil; in some places struck with pestles; / in some places they are cooked on heated iron slabs;
in some places they eat vomit, in some pus, in some blood, / in some feces, and in some flesh, amidst terribly foul stenches.
They are eaten by worms with fiery mouths here and there, / and amidst heaps of hair, blood, flesh, gore, fat, and bones,
the scattered corpses, devoid of bones, are devoured by worms visibly, / and torn to pieces by the beaks of crows, herons, and giant vultures,
in hundreds of millions of dense collisions with foul-smelling jackals, / and on saws, leaves made of stone, and boiling hot pans,
in the abodes of the Kūṭaśālmali tree with pillars of iron, oil, and fat, / and amidst pillars of blazing flames sharp as razors, thorns, and spikes,
in the boiling Vaitaraṇī filled with pus, in diverse manners, / and where the breasts of men and women are severed in the Sword-Leaved Forest,
in places terrible with the seizure of dreadful darkness, repeatedly / being thoroughly cooked and wailing through diverse and terrible torments;
with nooses tied around their necks and bound by serpents in some places, / crushed by mechanical presses, and dragged by their knees;
their backs, heads, and necks broken, their throats stiffened, most terrible, / made to wander in torturous chambers with bodies suited for torment—
sinners who committed wrongful acts are tormented, O king, crying out; / their wailing is accompanied by [remembrance of] sensory pleasures.
Whatever was done previously is experienced by all creatures; / association with the wives of others, though done for pleasure, yields sorrow.
Sensory pleasure for a moment becomes a giver of sorrow for many years. / O lord of kings, from your body, due to the morning bath in Mādhava
purified according to the injunction, the wind reached them, / and having obtained relief for a moment, they were refreshed by your radiance.
Because of that, those dwelling in hell became free from wailing. / Even hearing the name of the virtuous is said to bring happiness;
the touch of the wind that touches their body brings comfort. / Yama said: Hearing these words of the messengers, that king, a treasure of compassion,
replied to those messengers of Viṣṇu of wondrous deeds: / “The heart of the virtuous is indeed tender like fresh butter;
it melts visibly, just as [butter melts] when scorched by the heat of fire.” / The king said: “I cannot bring myself to go and torment afflicted beings, leaving them behind.
Fie upon that most sinful person who, though capable, does not destroy the distress of the afflicted! / If, by the touch of the breeze that has brushed against my body,
these creatures have become comfortable, then take me there. / Those men purify their mother and the earth,
who alleviate the burning distress of others, just as sandalwood soothes [fever]. / Those who suffer for the sake of helping others are truly fortunate.
They alone are virtuous in the world who destroy the sorrow of others, / for whom life-breaths are like blades of grass for the sake of ending the suffering of the afflicted.
By such men, dedicated to the welfare of others, is this earth sustained. / Whatever brings constant joy to the mind is heaven; hell is its opposite.”
"Therefore, the good are ever happy solely through the happiness of others. / Falling into hell here is preferable, separation from one's life is preferable,
but there is no happiness for a single moment without ending the distress of the distressed." / The messengers said: "Creatures, those sinners are cooked here in dreadful hell.
They live solely off their own past actions; here there is no room for delusion. / By those who made no gift, offered no oblation, took no bath at a holy site,
nor ever aided others with devotion, nor performed any excellent good deed, / by those who neither sacrificed, nor performed austerities, nor recited mantras with delight, O king,
they are cooked in those terrible hells in the next world. / Those of bad character, of wicked conduct, whose amusements and diet are censured,
injurers of others, committers of sins, pursuers of evil pastimes, / who rend the hearts of others with cutting words, those wicked people,
and those who take pleasure in the wives of others are cooked in hell. / Come now, O king; let us go to the temple of Hari.
It is not fitting for you, possessor of merit, to stay here any longer." / The king said: "If I am a doer of good deeds, O messengers, why have I been brought on this
hellish path of great terror? Or what is my supreme good deed? / Even I, dominated by desire, performed no such good deed.
How shall I go to the city of Hari? Indeed, I am in doubt." / The messengers said: "Truly, no good deed was performed by you whose self was overcome by desire;
you neither sacrificed with sacrifices, nor ate what remained of sacrifices. / However, because during the month of Mādhava, in accordance with the injunctions, for three years,
having bathed at dawn, impelled in former times by your guru's instruction, / you worshipped with devotion Viṣṇu, the lord of the universe, slayer of Madhu,
destroyer of hosts of great sins and severe sins, who is fond of his devotees— / by that single [observance], which is the sole essence of all dharma, O lord of men,
you are carried to the abode of merit, being worshipped by the hosts of the Maruts. / Mādhava, when worshipped, is the destroyer of even great sins;
likewise the month of Mādhava has been proclaimed for mortals according to the rule. / Just as a heap of straw is set ablaze by a spark,
so too the flood of sins is consumed by the morning bath in Vaiśākha. / Sins, even very great ones, hold sway in the body only so long
as one does not plunge into a holy water at dawn in the month of Mādhava. / The man who is engaged in the month of Vaiśākha with the prescribed observances,
freed from the floods of sin by devotion to Hari alone, will go to the abode of Acyuta. / Indeed, because no good deed was performed by you previously from birth,
on that account you were brought to the path leading to the place of hell, O ruler of men. / Therefore, O lord of the earth, swiftly with us and the hosts of the Maruts,
praised in an aerial car, go to the temple of Govinda."

5.102.m: Yama said: / "Then the king, an ocean of compassion, distressed by their sorrow, / spoke with humility to the messengers of glorious Hari, O Brahmin:
'The wise consider the protection of the frightened to be the true fruit / of power, noble birth, virtuous qualities, and merit.
If I have any merit, let these creatures go to heaven / by means of it, freed from misery; I will dwell in their place.'
Having heard these words of the truthful king, which were beneficial, / they, meditating on his truth and generosity, addressed the king:
The messengers said: 'By this speech and compassionate act of yours, O king, / an increase of your accumulated dharma has taken place in particular.
Bathing, giving, recitation of mantras, oblations, asceticism, worship of the gods, and the like / performed in the month of Mādhava—they know it to yield endless fruit.
The sacrificer and the giver play in heaven together with the thirty [gods] / at tanks with golden lotuses and beneath the wish-granting tree.
Sung of by hosts of celestial maidens, he attains delight. / From giving water and food, a man attains the auspicious world of Varuṇa.
The giver of a cow easily carries across seven generations. / Having given a horse, one goes to the world of the sun; a man who gives knowledge
goes to the world of Brahmā, and from the gift of gold, to the abode of the gods; / he who gives a maiden goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
He who, having bathed in the month of Mādhava, having given gifts and worshipped Mādhava, / attains all desires and goes to the imperishable state.
On one side are austerities, gifts, sacrifices, pressing rites, and other rituals; / on the other is the great month of Mādhava observed according to rule.
The good deed performed by you during even a single day of that month of Mādhava / in former times, O king, surpasses all gifts.
Out of compassion, give the merit of a single day, O protector of the earth, / to those suffering, being cooked in hell, O ocean of mercy!
There is no dharma equal to compassion, no austerity equal to compassion, / no gift equal to compassion, no friend equal to compassion.
The giver of merit always obtains merit multiplied a hundred thousand times; / especially out of compassion, the increase of your dharma will come from that.
The man who lifts the suffering of distressed beings— / he alone in the world is known as a doer of good deeds, born of a portion of Nārāyaṇa.
On the full moon in the month of Vaiśākha, the bathing, gifts, and other rites / performed by you at a holy site, O hero, destroying all sins—
give that to them in accordance with rule, having made lord Hari your witness, / and three times spoken, so that these may attain heaven from hell.
In former times, Śibi, an ocean of mercy, having given his own flesh out of compassion / for the sake of a dove, shines in heaven, an ocean of fame.
The royal sage Dadhīci too, having given the heap of his own bones, / obtained imperishable heaven and fame that is moonlight to the three worlds.
And the illustrious royal sage Sahasrajit, having abandoned his dear life / for the sake of a Brahmin, went to the unexcelled worlds.
Neither in heaven nor even in final liberation does a man attain that happiness / which arises from giving cessation of pain to a distressed creature; such is our thought.
Among all classes of givers, you have come foremost in former times, O king, / through this deed, bringing constant firmness of mind into your reckonings.
Seeing that your mind, dharma, compassion, and giving are completely unwavering, / enthusiasm is generated even by us, who speak of dharma.
If it pleases you, O king, then without delay / give to them that merit which burns away the sorrow of torment.'

Thus addressed, the compassionate one then made Gadādhara a witness
and granted them the threefold merit according to rule.
When that good deed arising from a single day of the month of Mādhava was given, / the creatures were freed from the torments of Yama;
having mounted excellent celestial aerial cars, they all went to heaven, / bowing, praising, and looking upon him, overjoyed.
Having received that merit given by the king, born of a single day of the month of Vaiśākha, / they all, freed from hell, went to heaven mounted on aerial cars—wondrous indeed!

Truly, the host of living beings on earth is manifold; the state of their arising is manifold in many ways; / likewise the joining of all karma is manifold, and manifold is the accumulation of the power of that karma.

He who obtained merit exceeding that particular [gift], being praised by hosts of sages and gods, / adorable to the attendants of the Lord of the Universe, went to the supreme state unattainable by the best of yogins.

5.103.m:
Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter in the Glorification of the Month of Vaiśākha in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.

The sages said:
"O Sūta, O Sūta of great wisdom, by you of exceedingly compassionate soul / the sin-destroying glorification of the month of Vaiśākha has been proclaimed,
and the observances for the slayer of Madhu in Mādhava have been spoken of by you: / worship, bathing, gifting, and so on, according to Vedic and Smṛti ordinances,
and how the god Mādhava, the destroyer of sins, is pleased. / Now we wish to hear the meditation on that great-souled one,
on Kṛṣṇa, dear to the host of devotees, which carries one across worldly existence."

Sūta said:
"Listen, all you sages, to [the meditation on] Kṛṣṇa, the self of the universe, / the very life of cows, cowherds, and cowherd women, who roams in Vṛndāvana.

Once, O best of twice-born, Nārada was questioned by Gautama; / he declared to him the meditation, which destroys sins; that I shall tell."

Nārada said:
"Adorned with the beauty of bending clusters of fresh sprouts on excellent trees gleaming with mead trickling from the fragrance of masses of blossoms,

entwined with charming creepers bearing fully blown fresh flower-clusters, / one of sharp intellect should continually remember auspicious, lovely Vṛndāvana,

its interior made resounding with humming coming from the mouths of bees moving about, charming as they taste the nectar of blooming flowers,
filled with the calls of birds such as doves, parrots, mynas, and cuckoos here and there, and agitated with the dancing of peacocks;

served unceasingly by breezes bearing spray from the tossing waves of the daughter of Kalinda, made grayish with heaps of pollen from the interiors of wide-open lotuses, which arouse passion and agitate the garments of the playful women of Vraja;

and within it one should contemplate a lofty wish-fulfilling tree, whose fresh shoots are coral, whose leaves are emeralds, whose bud-clusters have the luster of pearls, which bears various fruits of ruby, which is massive, ever attended by all seasons, and bestows desires;

further, the wise man, freed from the six waves [of suffering], unwearied, should meditate beneath it upon a golden ground, radiant like the rising sun upon a mountain of fine golden peaks, raining showers of nectar, with a floor of blazing gems, bright with heaps of flower pollen;

having contemplated an eight-petaled red lotus upon an exalted yogic seat set on that jeweled pavement, / then, in its center, gleaming like the rising sun, one should contemplate Mukunda comfortably seated:

resembling in luster Indra's thunderbolt, crushed collyrium, a mass of clouds, and a freshly blossomed blue lotus; / with a dense mass of curled, very glossy black hair; crowned with a charming, shining crest of peacock feathers;

adorned with an abundance of celestial-tree flowers cherished by bees; with ear-ornaments of freshly expanded blue water lilies; / with a bright mark of gorocanā on the expanse of his forehead, where restless bees hover; with brilliant eyebrow-bows;

his lovely face like the spotless orb of the full autumn moon; with eyes wide as lotus petals; / with mirror-like cheeks shining with the rays of jewel-glittering makara-shaped earrings; with a raised, beautiful nose;

with lips far more lovely than red vermilion; lighting up the quarters with the glow of his gentle smile like the moon, kunda flowers, and mandāra; / with a neck beautiful as a conch, shining with an exquisite necklace fashioned from a multitude of wild corals and flowers;

his shoulders adorned with a dangling garland of parijāta blossoms humming with intoxicated wandering bees; / his broad, stout chest radiant like the sky with rows of star-like pearl necklaces, where the sun-like Kaustubha gem gleams;

clearly marked with the auspicious Śrīvatsa mark; with high shoulders; with well-formed, plump, rounded arms reaching down to his knees; / with a handsome belly, a noble and deep navel, and a line of delicate hair charming as a swarm of female bees;

wearing armlets, bracelets, rings, necklaces, girdles, anklets, and belly-bands fashioned from various jewels; / his slender body golden-yellow with divine unguents; the curve of his hips wrapped in yellow garments;

whose charming thighs and knees are rounded, with lovely shanks; whose graceful, elevated forefeet outshine the beauty of a tortoise;
whose beautiful lotus feet have shining red petal-toes that gleam with a king of nails glistening like a ruby mirror—

charming with the soles of his reddish hands and feet distinctly marked with a fish, goad, disc, conch, banner, barley corn, lotus, and thunderbolt; / his limbs formed from the concentrated essence of loveliness; the bodily charm of the god of love reproached by his beauty;
an ocean of boundless bliss, causing all beings to bow continuously with the divine melodies brought forth by his dancing fingers covering the holes of the flute held to his lotus mouth;

then, surrounded by cows whose eyes are dissolved in his lotus face, whose gait is slow and languid from the weight of their udders, / with tips of grass shoots remaining between their biting teeth, and their tail-vines hanging down;

and by young calves whose mouths are motionless, filled from sucking at dripping udders, charming with frothy milk firmly trickling out, / who have raised their pairs of ears high toward the lovely sweet song brought forth by the flute;

and by herds of bull-calves and heifer-calves plump with fat, with large dewy dewlaps and uplifted tails, / with restless hooftips tapping in eager anticipation of soft playful butts of their young horns upon their heads.

with great mature bulls agitated throughout the compass by their lowing, weary under the heavy burden of their broad humps, / with their large nostrils flared and raised in intoxication by the nectar of the flute's song, drank in by their uplifted ears;

and by cowherds of equal virtues, character, age, charm, and dress, their flutes and lutes swelling with sweet soft tones, / dedicated to singing skillfully in low, high, and middle pitches, adept at performing lovely dances with their swaying creeper-like arms;

and surrounded by charming little boys wandering about, their jangling bells tinkling, tied around the slopes of their plump hips and shanks, / adorned with lovely ornaments fashioned from hyena claws, speaking sweet, indistinct words.

Then, by lovely, graceful cowherd maidens, made slow [in gait] by their thick braids and heavy hips, / possessing three folds on their waists bent under the weight of heavy breasts, adorned with rising lines of bodily hair;

the creeper-like limbs of whom were adorned with spotless, delightful, bristling hairs standing on end like buds, / as the tree of Love sprouted within them through the nectar of his exceedingly charming and beautiful flute-playing;

over whom spread a continuous stream of heavy drops of perspiration, like sprays from the swift-moving ripples / of an ocean of passion aroused by the moonlight of his exceedingly charming, gentle smile;

whose vital parts were all struck, their bodies undone, by the shower of Kāma's arrows—his sharp glances released from the bow of his most graceful, gentle eyebrows— / and through whose bodies coursed the pain of unbearable trembling;
eager to drink the nectar of the beauty of his exceedingly charming attire and form, / carrying streams of the waters of love, their lotus eyes languid and wandering;

constantly attended by swarms of bees greedy for the dripping honey-nectar of the blossoming flowers falling from their loosening braids of hair, / their soft words stammering in the intoxication of love, the radiance of their hips flashing with shifting silk robes whose inner knots were slipping from their trembling girdles;

the directions filled with the sounds of their bejeweled anklets striking as their charming lotus feet stumbled, / their lower lips trembling, their bud-like lotus eyes with fine lashes flickering, their earrings flashing;

their reddish sprout-like lips fading from the heat of the wind of their long-drawn sighs, / their lotus hands radiant with various offerings—[he was] constantly attended on all sides by these maidens.

His entire body was honored with garlands of blooming blue water-lilies from their long, roving, dark eyes, the dwelling-place of various graces; / he wore a charming garland, delighting the lover intoxicated with the sweet nectar dripping from their charming lotus faces.

Outside the circle of the gopīs, cowherds, and cattle, one should meditate in front of him upon the host of gods seeking spiritual wealth, headed by Viriñci, the Three-eyed Lord, and Śatamanyu, intent on hymns of praise;

likewise on the right upon the multitude of sages devoted to Vedic recitation out of a firm desire for dharma; / and behind him upon Sanaka and the other foremost yogis desiring liberation through meditative absorption;

and on the left upon the yakṣas, siddhas, gandharvas, vidyādharas, and cāraṇas with their beloved consorts, / together with the kinnaras, and the foremost apsarases seeking fulfillment through dance, song, and music.

[One should meditate upon] me, born of Druhiṇa, white as a conch, the moon, and jasmine, knower of all traditional lore, my mass of matted hair yellow as a flash of lightning, / desiring pure devotion fixed upon his lotus feet, having utterly cast aside all other attachment,
pleasing [him] with delightful melodic scales based on the three vocal registers and the seven musical modes, accompanied by diverse tonal nuances, / filled with great devotion in the sky.

Having thus meditated upon the son of Nanda and upon oneself, a man of sharp and clear intellect, with his very mind, through blameless offerings such as water for washing the feet and so forth,
should worship him repeatedly with devotion, and through external splendors upon his own body; thus all that was desired has been proclaimed, O best of earthly gods.

5.104.m: The sages said: / "Speak again, O highly fortunate one, of the wondrous deeds of Rāma, / the essence of Rāma's glorification, which brings delight to the devotees."
Sūta said: / "Having performed the horse sacrifice, the best of rites, the son of Daśaratha, as he was,
engaged in worldly affairs and skilled in the precepts of the scriptures, / while Śaṅkara, the great soul, wishing to go to Ayodhyā,
dwelt on the bank of the Sarayū together with the goddess Pārvatī. / The sages, approaching that Śaṅkara of universal form,
the great souls headed by Kaśyapa, questioned him of boundless splendor: / 'Welcome to you, O best of sages! Whence have you come with your wife?
What is the purpose of your coming? To which country do you intend to go?' / Śaṅkara said: 'I am a brāhmaṇa named Śambhu, dwelling on the snowy mountain.
I am going to see Rāghava; I have great business with him. / That king calls me, being devoted to listening to the Purāṇas.
You also come along; Rāghava will be well pleased.' / Then those sages and Śambhu went, desiring to see Rāma.
Knowing that they had arrived, Vasiṣṭha informed Rāma. / Then, rising up swiftly, he went out accompanied by his family priest.
He honored all those sages with water for reception, water for the feet, and the rest; / then the tamer of foes had them all enter the royal palace.
Having offered a seat to each, after welcoming them as they sat, / the tiger among the Raghus honored those sages in due order.
Delighting them with sweet speech, he addressed them seated there: / Glorious Rāma said: 'Today my birth has borne fruit; today the fruit of my asceticism has been attained.
Today the time for the fruit of my study of sciences has arrived; / today my ancestors are satisfied, and my kingdom has borne fruit.
Today my conduct has borne fruit; today my learning has borne fruit.' / To the king speaking thus, the brāhmaṇas headed by Kaśyapa
spoke very pleasing words to Rāma, whose eyes are like lotus petals. / The sages said: / 'This brāhmaṇa Śambhu has arrived, skilled in all the scriptures,
knowing the truth of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, devoted to the welfare of all beings, / an eternal resident of Kailāsa, resolute in asceticism,
equal to Brahmā in spiritual luster, the best of the knowers of Brahman, / like Hari in affection for brāhmaṇas, equal to Śaṅkara in granting favor.
Such is this brāhmaṇa bull Śambhu of great splendor, / knower of the eighteen Purāṇas, skilled in Mīmāṃsā and Nyāya.
Only through the weight of your fortune has this best of sages arrived. / Summoned by you, O lord, the excellent sage has come from Kailāsa.
Therefore ask, O fortunate one, the excellent narration of the Purāṇa. / Desirous of hearing it, we too have reached you today, O delight of the Raghus.
Even if a man has mastered the Vedas and knows the meaning of all scriptures, / if he has not heard the Purāṇas, his understanding is not complete.'
Sūta said: / "Addressed thus by the sages who see the truth, the best of the Raghus / obtained unequaled joy, eager to hear the Purāṇa.
Glorious Rāma said: / 'The manner of worshipping the liṅga, and also the glorification of the liṅga, / the glorification of Maheśa's name, and the glorification of worship;
the glorification of bowing, and the glorification of sight, / the glorification of the gift of water, and of the gift of incense, O best of men;'
as well as the giving of lamps, perfumes, and so forth, and the glorification of flowers; / the sin-destroying story of various narratives and legendary histories;
and dharma, worldly gain, desire, and liberation, as well as the means to them, O steadfast observer of vows: / all that I wish to hear from you, O best of excellent sages.
Śambhu said: / Rāma, Rāma, mighty-armed one! You are meritorious, O Rāghava, / since you, attached to kingship, have developed delight in listening to the Purāṇa.
It comes from serving the great, O Rāma, and from resorting to sacred places. / That alone is a tongue which sings of Śiva; that alone is a mind which is offered to him;
those hands alone are praiseworthy which perform his worship; / that birth and body alone are truly fortunate among endless births,
wherein you shine with hair standing on end from chanting the names of Hara. / I am fulfilled, O great king, whose intellect has pursued your inquiry.
Immediately afterward, couriers arrived, weary with haste. / Taking the letter from their hands, the best of Raghus read it.
Rāma reflected in his mind: “How did this happen?” / Then Śambhu, disguised as a brāhmaṇa together with the Goddess, addressed Rāma:
“What are you worrying about, descendant of Kakutstha, even while the sages reside before you?” / Hearing his words, Rāghava questioned the foremost sages.
The glorious Rāma said: / “How is it that Bibhīṣaṇa has been bound with chains by men, / even after beholding the Liṅga of Śiva, Rāmeśvara, established by me? Ah!
By the crooked and wicked Drāviḍas? Let that be examined by yourself!” / Having reflected, those best of sages were unable to understand it even slightly.
They said to Rāma: “We do not know.” Then Rāma said: / “Consulting the Purāṇa according to the rule, declare all of that, O best of men!
And the cause of your ignorance should be investigated after that: / which Purāṇa should be consulted, and which one should likewise be avoided?
What kind of verse is commendable, and what kind would be otherwise? / And in what sorts of matters should what kind of worshipper [act]?
And by what sort of devotees should worship be performed for discerning a decision?” / Hearing these words of Rāma, those best of twice-borns
replied to that best of Raghus, whose mind was agitated by anxiety: / “We are not the best of speakers, O Rāma; rather, let the knower of Purāṇas examine it.”
Hearing that, Rāghava questioned Śambhu with humility. / He too, hearing his words, replied with great wisdom.

Śambhu said: / “One who makes a living through the Purāṇa is worthy of worship if he has studied his own Vedic branch, is pure, / knows the truth of Mīmāṃsā, is learned in the Veda, and censures falsehood;
who looks upon all gods with equal vision, is devoted to Śiva, / recites the Śatarudrīya, maintains a sacred fire, and is an eminent reciter.
A wise man, especially a follower of the Yajurveda, should worship the book / written on auspicious palm-leaves, endowed with the divine script,
which contains the elaborate arrangement of metres and pauses, alongside the syllable Om. / At the edge of the two lines, formerly and above, the line that joins the front of the Praṇava
should thus be one line; next to it is the letter 'a': / beginning from the upper part, hanging downward with an angle—
that should be known as the letter 'ā'. By the right line of the headband, / having two curved dots on the left, it is proclaimed as the letter 'i'.
With its left top-line hanging down, the letter 'ī' is declared. / On every letter there is an uncurved top-line, except on the Praṇava.
On that [letter], another hanging line resembles a sickle at its end: / that is celebrated as the letter 'u'; and with two sickles, it is 'ū'.
In this manner the goddess of speech has spoken all the other letters. / A Purāṇa written in this very script is indeed praised.
The Brahma, Padma, Vaiṣṇava, and the Mārtaṇḍa spoken by Nārada, / the Mārkaṇḍeya, then the Āgneya, Kūrma, and Vāmana,
the Gāruḍa, that named Laiṅga, the Skānda, Mātsya, Nṛsiṃha; / likewise, O Rāma, the Kapila Purāṇa is declared,
the Vārāha, and the Brahmavaivarta is praised for omens; / the Śaiva, Bhāgavata, Daurga, and the Bhaviṣyottara,
and the Bhaviṣya and minor Purāṇas; but one should avoid other texts. / Untying the manuscript, having placed it purified on a jeweled throne,
wearing washed garments, having bathed, pure, free from anger, and free from distress, / first worshipping oneself and making the formal resolution,
one should meditate on the white Sarasvatī of serene countenance, / holding a goad, a rosary, a noose, and a book.
One should meditate on the tranquil Śiva, whose form resembles cow's milk, three-eyed, riding a bull, / with a smiling face, clad in white garments,
crowned with a diadem, with a pair of upper arms holding a deer and the gesture of fearlessness, / with the gesture of exposition in the lower right hand, and granting boons with the left,
richly adorned with various jewels, seated on a lotus with Girijā taking up half his body, / whose lotus feet are meditated upon by many foremost sages,
praised by the embodied Vedas and Purāṇas, / and whose lotus feet are served by all other worlds.
Having thus meditated, the worshipper should properly begin the worship at the outset. / The consecrated water pot is blessed with the mantra 'Āpo vā idam…'
Taking that water, he should consecrate it while it is in the vessel / with the mantra 'Tat sat brahma', praising it with the Praṇava.
He should invoke himself and all vessels with the words 'iti'. / The sixteen-part worship of Bhāratī is done with the triplet beginning 'Yad vāk…',
or he may do it with the Puruṣa hymn, or worship with the Gāyatrī. / He should worship the Purāṇa saying: 'Om, obeisance to the venerable so-and-so Purāṇa.'
Bringing dūrvā grass with the mantra beginning 'Kāṇḍāt…', he should worship it / saying: 'Om, obeisance to the venerable goddess Dūrvā.'
There should be worship of the world-protectors, and then the worship of a maiden. / Auspicious are those above five years and under ten years of age,
or one who has not yet attained puberty; he should worship her with diligence / using perfumes, flowers, unhusked barley grains, incenses, lamps, betel leaves, and ornaments.
The worshipper should also have this maiden recite this mantra:
“Speak the truth, speak what is pleasing; O venerable Sarasvatī, salutation, salutation to you!”
In accordance with the order of the Gāyatrī, he should place a pair of dūrvā stalks. / Beneath the presence of the manuscript, with the verse 'Sahasraparama…',
the discerning man should place three pairs of dūrvā grass in her hand. / She should then insert three sticks sequentially into the fold of the manuscript.
With the words 'May it be dismissed', he should again offer [it] saying: 'Obeisance to Śiva and Śivā.' / The middle verse between the two folios indicates the success of the undertaking.
If the completion of the verse occurs on the previous folio, O Rāghava, / he should read the verse on the subsequent folio, and having analyzed it, state the meaning.
The wise man should read slowly and explain slowly. / Haste should not be made here, for speech becomes angry at haste.
A fourth of a ghaṭikā should elapse, or even greater absence of haste. / One should not rush the speaker, the twice-born who is to clarify the matter to be known.
Having analyzed the reading of the verse and settled the meaning in his mind, / contrary [speech] should not be uttered after analyzing it, O joy of Raghu.
Whether proper or improper, if that worshipper, being a virtuous twice-born, / should read another verse, abandoning what is written in the manuscript,
that should indeed be understood as it is; dispute is not commended. / For that verse has arrived by fate, and fate is indeed stronger.
Just as in omen-voices, there is no fault of the twice-born. / Astonishment should not be felt, for the path of destiny is crooked.”

When there is an inversion of words or [a verse appears] on an upper folio in water,
one should disregard that directive and read the second [verse] thereafter.

Then the third [verse] should be read, and from that an evaluation should be made.
Those [syllables] ending in a visarga, initial [letters], and the fifth letters of the classes other than the labials,

a verse free from marks of praise is commended in omens.
The beginning of a chapter, its conclusion, a blank folio, useless writing,

repeating what has been said, also a double praise,
a burnt folio, lost writing, and ambiguous syllables—

these are always to be avoided in an omen by the wise.
A query should indeed be known as twofold, through the division into agitated and calm.

The calm is also to be known as twofold, by origin, maintenance, and growth.
Among them, the calm is commended when marked by the aforesaid characteristics.

Different kinds of undertakings useful to mortals are now described:
undertaking an affair for someone, a person may also become an inquirer.

He then makes an inquiry: 'Coming together, what does he remember here?'
That folio is then to be held, and on that [subject] a folio is commended.

Or else supreme dispassion combined with forbearance [is indicated].
Wherever it may be seen, [if it is] only a quarter-verse of praise,

and setting aside another [matter], it brings good fortune in that affair.
'The dead man grasps the meaning of speech'—such a query brings misfortune.

In a dispute, when victory is queried, [a verse] indicating victory is desired.
A creation [passage] is also praised here; in a harsh one, victory comes through suffering.

In a calm [passage], [victory comes] through peaceful means, but in a mixed one, there will be frustration.
As for a description of a city or the like, whether middling or excellent,

in the expectation of strife, when describing erotic love,
and in anxiety about maintaining a kingdom, a symbol of royal power brings auspiciousness.

Whatever is appropriate for someone, the wise should examine it accordingly.
In matters of praise and dispassion, dissolution of the affair is declared.

Through an error, little success in the undertaking occurs, and it does not reach completion.
Its alteration of another sense [produces] another state, O Rāma, in the deliberation on peace.

An ending with a visarga and an inversion of the first half [indicate misfortune] for the future.
Failure of what was intended occurs at the conclusion of a chapter;

at the conclusion of a section or the like, destruction of that undertaking will occur.
Therefore, in such a fault, there is an inversion of the omen.

When sneezing occurs, when a book falls, or when one is struck on the head or elsewhere,
the speaker incurs disrespect; from that, the omen is destroyed.

Therefore, in such a fault, one should avoid the omen.
In a simile, O Rāma, an appearance of an effect occurs, but not in reality.

Where lineage is mentioned elsewhere, creation yields middling results.
Praise is commended somewhere in determining an undertaking endowed with virtue;

and in marriage, medicine, gift-giving, business, and agriculture,
appropriate praise, O Rāma, is no fault even in completion.

Praise that is inappropriate does not accomplish the undertaking.
Similarly, in the case of a verse whose meaning is unintelligible, disregarded in Purāṇas and the like,

in flight, in the loss of country, when disease arises,
and in this defeat by thieves and the like, there is terrible destruction of the undertaking.

If the query is calm, so the knowers of the past declare.
Rāma said: 'How will a knower of the Purāṇa recite a verse whose meaning is unintelligible?'

'It is unsaid; it was not properly heard by the listeners'—such is the conviction.
Therefore let it be illustrated for me, and let its meaning also be considered;

even if it is partly unintelligible, you should speak of it here, O learned one.'
Śambhu said: 'The honeys and honeys here, spring, the honey-eater, honey,

by honey, by honey, today's meaning, and horns, and horns.'
This verse, whose meaning is unintelligible, is not commended in an omen.

'Rutī rute rute rorau rīrī rāraṃ rarīraram—
thus acts the pure-minded brāhmaṇa, the guest of Brahmā.'

This verse, unintelligible in parts, is not praised in an omen.
Such are the verses in the Purāṇas, O best of the Raghu lineage;

they exist, yet they have no commentary; recitation of them is merely [prescribed].
There is no flaw in the speaker or the listener during vows and observances.

Purāṇas, like the Veda, are not to be questioned as to how they can be so;
through the force of three repetitions and the like, an understanding of the meaning arises upon reflection.

Reflecting upon the meaning of the verse and the procedure in ultimate truth:
there the verse is strong, but the procedure is lighter than that.

On a useless folio, there is wasted effort; on a burnt folio, destruction;
on a folio where maintenance is interrupted, there is disorder in the undertaking.

On a decayed folio, expense is declared; likewise when the script is lost;
on a useless syllable, wasted effort; upon repetition, disagreement.

In a simile, that undertaking almost succeeds, yet it does not succeed;
or success comes after delay; but when the syllables are unclear,

the undertaking falls into doubt, even on the days appointed.
One should not consult an omen in the Purāṇa every day, O king.

Nor should one consult the Purāṇa while getting up after eating.
After performing worship at night on the preceding day,

in the morning on the following day, regarding the omen, O delight of the Raghu lineage,
the examination should be made afterward, or at that very time.

Through the specificity of the procedure and the like, one should state the specific omen.
In all auspicious undertakings, rites for the deceased, ancestral offerings, and the like must be avoided;

infliction of punishment, a curse, the overthrow of lands,
the unmitigated killing of living beings by demons and evil creatures;

conflagration, building of a temple, spitting, vomiting, weeping,
laughter, disgust, sorrow, bad dreams, delusion, sins;

the filling of cloth and the like, affliction, quarrel, and death;
the arrival of cruel people, and fear of the great.

These and other procedures one should avoid.
In the consideration of acquiring fortune, the creation of kings brings happiness;

the rising of planets and the pacification of disease are also praised here.
What is the use of speaking much on this? One should consider each respective conjunction.

Among all the Purāṇas, the Skānda is praised in this regard;
some desire the Vaiṣṇava, while others [desire] the Rāmāyaṇa.

In truth and other [matters], all faults are indeed faults in the Vaiṣṇava;
in the Skānda and in the Rāmāyaṇa, there is faultiness, but it is slight.

However, the Vaiṣṇava cannot be worshipped by just anyone;
if it should be worshipped by one devoid of virtuous conduct,

then it turns out as though inauspicious; the omen does not succeed at all,
just as a bull tethered to a branch in [an area] endowed with all customary duties.

Sūta said: Thus instructed by the brāhmaṇa Śambhu, Rāghava then
proceeded to [consult] an omen for the examination of Vibhīṣaṇa.

Rāghava spoke these words to Vasiṣṭha, who knew all truths
and was skilled in the Purāṇas: 'Let the Purāṇa be examined.'

Vasiṣṭha also spoke to Rāma: 'In the presence of this sage,
I have no ability, O Rāma, to speak or to examine.'

Rāma then said to Śambhu, whose face was looked upon by the sage:
'You also know the truth and are skilled in the Purāṇas;

therefore tell the omen found in the Purāṇa regarding my undertaking.'
Saying 'So be it,' Śambhu, having become pure, became the worshipper.

Having duly worshipped the Skānda, and having made an inquiry truly thus:
'Is my devotee Vibhīṣaṇa bound with a chain?'
These three directive verses were then seen in three ways.
Having bound the ocean, that lord of the Raghus besieged the rulers of night-wanderers in the city; / issuing forth to do battle, they came forth before Laṅkā, with Atikāya at their head.
